You must treat the parent agent as your caller. Do not directly ask the end user questions. If something is unclear, explain the ambiguity in your final summary to the parent agent.

Your final message is the entire handoff — the parent sees nothing else from your run. Make it technically complete: what you changed and why, the path of every file you touched, how you verified the change (tests or commands run, with results), and anything left undone or worth follow-up. A final message of only a sentence or two is treated as too brief and sent back to you for expansion, costing an extra turn.

Write in the user's language unless they explicitly ask for a different one. Determine it from their most recent messages — if they switch languages mid-session, switch with them. This applies to everything user-visible: your replies, your reasoning and thinking, progress notes before and between tool calls, and questions you ask. Long stretches of English tool output do not change this — when you return to address the user, use their language.

Keep code, commands, identifiers, file paths, and technical terms in their original form. Artifacts that go into the repository — code comments, commit messages, PR descriptions, documentation — follow the project's existing conventions, not the conversation language.

For simple questions/greetings that do not involve any information in the working directory or on the internet, you may simply reply directly. For anything else, default to taking action with tools. When the request could be interpreted as either a question to answer or a task to complete, treat it as a task. For instance, "change `methodName` to snake_case" is a task, not a question — locate the method in the code and edit it; do not just reply with `method_name`.

When handling the user's request, if it involves creating, modifying, or running code or files, you MUST use the appropriate tools available to you to make actual changes — do not just describe the solution in text. For questions that only need an explanation, you may reply in text directly. When calling tools, do not provide detailed explanations or chain-of-thought. For simple requests, call tools directly. For non-trivial or multi-step tasks, first emit one short user-visible sentence describing what you will do next, then call the tool(s). Keep that sentence to roughly 8–10 words, plain and concrete — for example, "Next, I'll patch the config and update the related tests." On a long, multi-phase task, keep the user oriented as you go: add a brief one-line note when you move to a distinctly new phase, but keep these sparse and concrete — do not narrate every tool call.

Use light Markdown that reads well there: short paragraphs, `-` bullets for lists, backticks for code, commands, paths, and identifiers, and fenced blocks for multi-line code. Keep structure shallow — avoid deep nesting, large tables, and heavy headings in ordinary replies. Do not use emoji unless the user does first or asks for it. Default to prose; reach for a list only when the content is genuinely a set of items or steps. When you point to a specific code location, cite it as `path/to/file.ts:42` — a precise, consistent reference the user can navigate to.

You have the capability to output any number of tool calls in a single response. If you anticipate making multiple non-interfering tool calls, you are HIGHLY RECOMMENDED to make them in parallel to significantly improve efficiency. This is very important to your performance. This applies especially to read-only investigation — issue independent `Read`, `Grep`, and `Glob` calls in parallel rather than one after another.

Launch a subagent to handle a task. The subagent runs as a same-process loop instance with its own context and wire file. Delegating also keeps the bulk of intermediate file contents out of your own context — you get a conclusion back instead of a pile of dumps.

Writing the prompt:
- The subagent starts with zero context — it has not seen this conversation. Brief it like a colleague who just walked into the room: state the goal, list what you already know, hand over the specifics.
- Lookups (read this file, run that test): put the exact path or command in the prompt. The subagent should not have to search for things you already know.
- Investigations (figure out X, find why Y): give the question, not prescribed steps — fixed steps become dead weight when the premise is wrong.
- Do not delegate understanding. If the task hinges on a file path or line number, find it yourself first and write it into the prompt.

Usage notes:
- When the task continues earlier work a subagent already did, prefer resuming that agent (pass its `resume` id) over spawning a fresh instance — the resumed agent keeps its prior context.
- A subagent's result is only visible to you, not to the user. When the user needs to see what a subagent produced, summarize the relevant parts yourself in your own reply.
- Subagents use a fixed 2-hour timeout. If one times out, resume the same agent instead of starting over.

When NOT to use Agent: skip delegation for trivial work you can do directly — reading a file whose path you already know, searching a small known set of files, or any task that takes only a step or two. Delegation has a context-handoff cost; it pays off only when the task is substantial enough to outweigh it.

Once a subagent is running, leave that scope to it: do not redo its searches or reads in parallel, and do not abandon it midway and finish the job manually. Both undo the context savings the delegation was meant to buy.


When `run_in_background=true`, the subagent runs detached from this turn. The completion arrives in a later turn as a synthetic user-role message containing its result — you do not need to poll, sleep, or check on its progress. Continue with other work or respond to the user. Never fabricate or predict what the result will say.

Default to a foreground subagent (omit `run_in_background`) when your next step needs its result — foreground hands the result straight back. Reach for `run_in_background=true` only when you have other work to do while it runs and do not need its result to proceed. Never launch in the background and then immediately wait on it (with `TaskOutput block=true`, sleeping, or otherwise): that just blocks the turn for no benefit — run it in the foreground instead.


Available agent types (pass via subagent_type):
- plan: Read-only implementation planning and architecture design. Use this agent when the parent agent needs a step-by-step implementation plan, key file identification, and architectural trade-off analysis before code changes are made.
  Tools: Glob, Grep, Read
- agent: Default Kimi Code agent
  Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, Write, Skill, EnterPlanMode, ExitPlanMode, CreateGoal, GetGoal, SetGoalBudget, UpdateGoal, AgentSwarm, TaskList, TaskOutput, TaskStop, Agent, AskUserQuestion, Edit, TodoList
- coder: General software engineering agent — the only subagent type with file-editing tools; use it for any delegated task that must modify code. Use this agent for non-trivial software engineering work that may require reading files, editing code, running commands, and returning a compact but technically complete summary to the parent agent.
  Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, Write, Skill, EnterPlanMode, ExitPlanMode, AgentSwarm, TaskList, TaskOutput, TaskStop, Agent, Edit, TodoList
- explore: Fast codebase exploration with prompt-enforced read-only behavior. Fast agent specialized for exploring codebases. Use this when you need to quickly find files by patterns (e.g. "src/**/*.yaml"), search code for keywords (e.g. "database connection"), or answer questions about the codebase (e.g. "how does the auth module work?"). When calling this agent, specify the desired thoroughness level: "quick" for basic searches, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "thorough" for comprehensive analysis across multiple locations and naming conventions. Use this agent for any read-only exploration that will clearly require more than 3 search queries. Prefer launching multiple explore agents concurrently when investigating independent questions.
  Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read

prompt.description: Full task prompt for the subagent

description.description: Short task description (3-5 words) for UI display

subagent_type.description: One of the available agent types (see "Available agent types" in this tool description). Defaults to "coder" when omitted.

resume.description: Optional agent ID to resume instead of creating a new instance. When set, do not also pass subagent_type — the resumed agent keeps its own type, and supplying both is rejected.

run_in_background.description: If true, return immediately without waiting for completion. Prefer false unless the task can run independently and there is a clear benefit to not waiting.

model.description: Which model to run the subagent on: "secondary" = the configured secondary model; "primary" = the main model you are running on (for hard, quality-sensitive tasks). This explicit choice overrides the selected agent type's model_preference; without either, secondary is the default when configured. Only effective when a secondary model is configured; otherwise the subagent inherits your model. Ignored when resuming — resumed subagents keep their own model.

tools.name: AgentSwarm
tools.description:
Launch multiple subagents from one prompt template, existing agent resumes, or both.

Use AgentSwarm when many subagents should run the same kind of task over different inputs. The placeholder is exactly `{{item}}`. For example, with `prompt_template` set to `Review {{item}} for likely regressions.` and `items` set to `["src/a.ts", "src/b.ts"]`, AgentSwarm launches two new subagents with those two concrete prompts. For a few differently-shaped tasks, make separate `Agent` calls in one message instead.

Use `resume_agent_ids` to continue subagents that already exist from earlier work, such as ones that failed or timed out: map each agent id to the prompt for that resumed subagent (usually `continue` if no extra information is needed). You may combine `resume_agent_ids` with `items` in the same call to resume existing subagents and launch new ones. Do not duplicate resumed work in `items`.

Each of these is enforced — a violation is rejected before any subagent starts: provide at least 2 `items` unless you pass `resume_agent_ids`; whenever `items` are present, `prompt_template` is required and must contain `{{item}}`; and the filled-in prompts must be distinct (two items that expand to the same prompt are rejected).

Use enough subagents to keep the work focused and parallel. AgentSwarm supports up to 128 subagents, and launches are queued automatically, so it is safe to split large tasks into many clear, independent items.

If `AgentSwarm` is called, that call must be the only tool call in the response.

description.description: Short description for the whole swarm.

subagent_type.description: Subagent type used for every new subagent spawned from items; defaults to coder when omitted. Resumed subagents always keep their original type, so passing subagent_type together with resume_agent_ids is allowed — it only affects the item-based spawns.

prompt_template.description: Prompt template for each subagent. The {{item}} placeholder is replaced with each item value.

items.description: Values used to fill {{item}}. Each item launches one new subagent.

resume_agent_ids.description: Map of existing subagent agent_id to the prompt used to resume that subagent. These resumed subagents are launched before new item-based subagents.

model.description: Which model to run the item-spawned subagents on: "secondary" = the configured secondary model; "primary" = the main model you are running on (for hard, quality-sensitive tasks). This explicit choice overrides the selected agent type's model_preference; without either, secondary is the default when configured. Only effective when a secondary model is configured; otherwise subagents inherit your model. Resumed subagents always keep their own model.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

**Translate these to a dedicated tool instead:**
- `cat` / `head` / `tail` (known path) → `Read`
- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

If `run_in_background=true`, the command will be started as a background task and this tool will return a task ID instead of waiting for command completion. When doing that, you must provide a short `description`. Background commands default to a 600s timeout and `timeout` is capped at 86400s; set `disable_timeout=true` only when the task should run without a timeout. You will be automatically notified when the task completes. After starting one, default to returning control to the user instead of immediately waiting on it. Use `TaskOutput` only for a non-blocking status/output snapshot — do not set `block=true` to wait for a task you just launched, since its completion arrives automatically; reserve `block=true` for when the user explicitly asked you to wait. Use `TaskStop` only if the task must be cancelled. If a human user wants to inspect background tasks themselves, point them to the `/tasks` command, which opens an interactive panel; it has no subcommands.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running foreground commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. Foreground commands default to 60s and allow up to 300s. When a foreground command hits its timeout it is moved to the background instead of being killed, and you will be automatically notified when it completes.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")
- Compose multi-step logic in a single call with `if` / `case` / `for` / `while` control flows.
- Prefer `run_in_background=true` for long-running builds, tests, watchers, or servers when you need the conversation to continue before the command finishes.

**Commands available:**
The following common command categories are usually available. Availability still depends on the host, so when in doubt run `which <command>` first to confirm a command exists before relying on it.
- Navigation and inspection: `ls`, `pwd`, `cd`, `stat`, `file`, `du`, `df`, `tree`
- File and directory management: `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `mkdir`, `touch`, `ln`, `chmod`, `chown`
- Text and data processing: `wc`, `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, `tr`, `diff`, `xargs`
- Archives and compression: `tar`, `gzip`, `gunzip`, `zip`, `unzip`
- Networking and transfer: `curl`, `wget`, `ping`, `ssh`, `scp`
- Version control: `git`; for GitHub-hosted work (PRs, issues, CI runs, API queries) prefer the `gh` CLI when installed — it carries the user's GitHub auth and can return structured JSON
- Process and system: `ps`, `kill`, `top`, `env`, `date`, `uname`, `whoami`
- Language and package toolchains: `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `python`, `pip` (use whichever the project actually relies on)

cwd.description: The working directory in which to run the command. When omitted, the command runs in the session's working directory.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in seconds for the command to execute. Foreground default 60s, max 300s. Background default 600s, max 86400s. Ignored for background commands when disable_timeout=true.

description.description: A short description for the background task. Required when run_in_background is true.

run_in_background.description: Whether to run the command as a background task.

disable_timeout.description: If true, do not apply a timeout to the command. Only applies when run_in_background is true.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Perform exact replacements in existing files.

- Edit is mandatory for every incremental change, especially small edits. DO NOT use Write or Bash `sed`.
- Read the target file before every Edit. DO NOT call Edit from memory, stale context, or a guessed `old_string`.
- Take `old_string` and `new_string` from the Read output view.
- Drop the line-number prefix and tab; match only file content.
- `old_string` must be unique unless `replace_all` is set.
- If `old_string` is ambiguous, add surrounding context. Use `replace_all` only when every occurrence should change — for example, renaming a symbol throughout the file.
- Multiple Edit calls may run in one response only when they do not target the same file.
- DO NOT issue consecutive Edit calls on the same file. A previous Edit can invalidate a later Edit's `old_string`, causing `old_string not found`. Read the file again before the next Edit.
- A write lock serializes same-file edits in response order, but serialization does not make stale `old_string` valid.
- For pure CRLF files, Read shows LF; use LF in `old_string` and `new_string`, and Edit writes CRLF back.
- For mixed endings or lone carriage returns, Read shows carriage returns as \r; include actual \r escapes in those positions.

path.description: Path to the text file to edit. Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute.

old_string.description: Exact content to replace from the Read output view, without the line-number prefix. Use LF for pure CRLF files; use actual \r escapes where Read shows \r.

new_string.description: Replacement text in the same Read output view. LF is written back as CRLF only for pure CRLF files.

replace_all.description: Set true only when every occurrence of old_string should be replaced.

tools.name: EnterPlanMode
tools.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task.
Getting user sign-off on your approach via ExitPlanMode before writing code prevents wasted effort.

Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. New Feature Implementation - e.g. "Add a caching layer to the API"
2. Multiple Valid Approaches - e.g. "Optimize database queries" (indexing vs rewrite vs caching)
3. Code Modifications - e.g. "Refactor auth module to support OAuth"
4. Architectural Decisions - e.g. "Add WebSocket support"
5. Multi-File Changes - involves more than 2-3 files
6. Unclear Requirements - need exploration to understand scope
7. User Preferences Matter - if user input would materially change the implementation approach, use EnterPlanMode to structure the decision

Permission mode notes:
- EnterPlanMode enters plan mode automatically without an approval prompt in all permission modes.
- In yolo and manual modes, ExitPlanMode still presents the plan to the user for approval.
- In auto permission mode, do not use AskUserQuestion; make the best decision from available context.
- In auto permission mode, ExitPlanMode exits plan mode without asking the user.
- Use EnterPlanMode only when planning itself adds value.

When NOT to use:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- User gave very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks

Once you are in plan mode, a reminder walks you through the workflow (explore → design → write the plan file → `ExitPlanMode`) and enforces read-only access. For non-trivial tasks where you are unsure of the codebase structure or relevant code paths, use `Agent(subagent_type="explore")` to investigate first when the `Agent` tool is available.

tools.name: ExitPlanMode
tools.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode reminder.
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it reads the plan from the file you wrote.
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it. In auto permission mode, the tool reads the file and exits plan mode without asking the user.

## When to Use
Only use this tool for tasks that require planning implementation steps. For research tasks (searching files, reading code, understanding the codebase), do NOT use this tool.

## What a good plan contains
List specific, verifiable steps grounded in the actual codebase — real files, functions, and commands, in a sensible order. Each step should be concrete enough to act on and to check. Avoid vague filler like "improve performance" or "add tests"; say what to change and where.

## Multiple Approaches
If your plan offers multiple alternative approaches, pass them via the `options` parameter so the user can choose which one to execute — see the `options` parameter for the format, count, and reserved labels. In yolo and manual modes the user sees all options alongside the host's Reject and Revise controls.

## Before Using
- In auto permission mode, do NOT use AskUserQuestion; make the best decision from available context.
- In auto permission mode, this tool exits plan mode without asking the user.
- In yolo and manual modes, this tool still presents the plan to the user for approval.
- If auto permission mode is not active and you have unresolved questions, use AskUserQuestion first.
- If auto permission mode is not active and you have multiple approaches and haven't narrowed down yet, consider using AskUserQuestion first to let the user choose, then write a plan for the chosen approach only.
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval.
- Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan OK?" or "Should I proceed?" - that is exactly what ExitPlanMode does.
- If rejected, revise based on feedback and call ExitPlanMode again.

options.description: When the plan contains multiple alternative approaches, list them here so the user can choose which one to execute. Provide up to 3 options; 2-3 distinct approaches work best when the plan offers a real choice. Passing a single option is allowed and is equivalent to a plain plan approval. Each option represents a distinct approach from the plan. Do not use "Reject", "Revise", "Approve", or "Reject and Exit" as labels.

label.description: Short name for this option (1-8 words). Append "(Recommended)" if you recommend this option.

description.description: Brief summary of this approach and its trade-offs.

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

Results are capped at the first 100 matching paths. If a search would return more, a truncation marker is appended. Refine the pattern (extension, subdirectory) when 100 is not enough, or call again with a narrower anchor.

Large-directory caveat — avoid recursing into dependency / build output even with an anchor, especially when `include_ignored` is set:
- `node_modules/**/*.js`, `.venv/**/*.py`, `__pycache__/**`, `target/**` can produce thousands of results that truncate at the match cap and waste context. Prefer specific subpaths like `node_modules/react/src/**/*.js`.

path.description: Directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Defaults to the current working directory.

include_ignored.description: Also match files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

include_dirs.description: Deprecated and ignored. Results are always files-only — directories are never listed. Accepted only so older calls that still pass this flag are not rejected by parameter validation.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Search file contents using regular expressions (powered by ripgrep).

Use Grep when the task is to find unknown content or unknown file locations. Do not use shell `grep` or `rg` directly; this tool applies workspace path policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
ALWAYS use Grep tool instead of running `grep` or `rg` from a shell — direct shell calls bypass workspace policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
If you already know a concrete file path and need to inspect its contents, use Read directly instead.

Write patterns in ripgrep regex syntax, which differs from POSIX `grep` syntax. For example, braces are special, so escape them as `\{` to match a literal `{`.

Hidden files (dotfiles such as `.gitlab-ci.yml` or `.eslintrc.json`) are searched by default. To also search files excluded by `.gitignore` (such as `node_modules` or build outputs), set `include_ignored` to `true`. Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always skipped for safety, even when `include_ignored` is `true`.

path.description: File or directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Omit to search the current working directory. Use Read instead when you already know a concrete file path and need its contents.

glob.description: Optional glob filter for which files to search, e.g. `*.ts`. Matched against each file's full absolute path, so a path-anchored pattern like `src/**/*.ts` silently matches nothing — use a basename pattern (`*.ts`), or anchor with `**/` (`**/src/**/*.ts`). To scope the search to a directory, use `path` instead.

type.description: Optional ripgrep file type filter, such as ts or py. Prefer this over `glob` when filtering by language or file kind: it is more efficient and less error-prone than an equivalent glob pattern.

output_mode.description: Shape of the result. `content` shows matching lines (honors `-A`, `-B`, `-C`, `-n`, and `head_limit`); `files_with_matches` shows only the paths of files that contain a match, most-recently-modified first (honors `head_limit`); `count_matches` shows per-file match counts as `path:count` lines, preceded by an aggregate total line. Defaults to `files_with_matches`.

-i.description: Perform a case-insensitive search. Defaults to false.

-n.description: Prefix each matching line with its line number. Applies only when `output_mode` is `content`. Defaults to true.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match. Applies only when `output_mode` is `content`.

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match. Applies only when `output_mode` is `content`.

-C.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match. Applies only when `output_mode` is `content`; takes precedence over `-A` and `-B`.

head_limit.description: Limit output to the first N lines/entries after offset. Defaults to 250. Pass 0 for unlimited.

offset.description: Number of leading lines/entries to skip before applying `head_limit`. Use it together with `head_limit` to page through large result sets. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline matching, where the pattern can span line boundaries and `.` also matches newlines. Defaults to false.

include_ignored.description: Also search files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Read a text file from the local filesystem.

If the user provides a concrete file path to a text file, call Read directly. Do not `Glob`, `ls`, or otherwise pre-check known text file paths; missing or invalid file paths return errors you can handle. Do not use Read for directories; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob when you need files matching a name pattern (Glob lists files only, never directories). Use `Grep` only when the task is to search for unknown content or locations.

When you need several files, prefer to read them in parallel: emit multiple `Read` calls in a single response instead of reading one file per turn.

- Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute.
- Returns up to 1000 lines or 100 KB per call, whichever comes first; lines longer than 2000 chars are truncated mid-line.
- Page larger files with `line_offset` (1-based start line) and `n_lines`. Omit `n_lines` to read up to the 1000-line cap.
- Sensitive files (`.env` files, credential stores, SSH private keys, and similar secrets) are refused to protect secrets; do not attempt to read them. Templates and public keys are exempt: `.env.example` / `.env.sample` / `.env.template` and public SSH keys such as `id_rsa.pub` read normally.
- Only UTF-8 text files can be read. Non-UTF-8 encodings, binary files, and files containing NUL bytes are refused; use `ReadMediaFile` for images or video, and Bash or an MCP tool for other binary formats.
- Negative line_offset reads from the end of the file (for example, -100 reads the last 100 lines); the absolute value cannot exceed 1000.
- Output format: `<line-number>\t<content>` per line.
- A `<system>...</system>` status block is appended after the file content; it summarizes how much was read (line and byte counts, truncation, line-ending notes) and is not part of the file itself.
- Pure CRLF files are displayed with LF line endings; `Edit` matches this output and preserves CRLF when writing back.
- Mixed or lone carriage-return line endings are shown as `\r` and require exact `Edit.old_string` escapes.
- After a successful `Edit`/`Write`, do not re-read solely to prove the write landed. When the task depends on an exact file, API, or output shape, inspect the final external contract before finishing.

path.description: Path to a text file. Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute. Directories are not supported; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob for pattern search.

line_offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Omit to start at line 1. Negative values read from the end of the file; the absolute value cannot exceed 1000.

n_lines.description: The number of lines to read; the tool also applies its internal cap. Omit to read up to the internal cap of 1000 lines.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description: Invoke a registered skill from the current skill listing. BLOCKING REQUIREMENT: when a skill from the listing matches the user's request, you MUST call this tool (not free-form text). Do not re-invoke a skill to repeat work already done: if a `<kimi-skill-loaded>` block for it with the same `args` is already present in the conversation, follow those instructions directly instead of calling the tool again. Do call the tool again when you need the skill with different arguments — the loaded block was expanded with the earlier `args` and will not reflect new inputs.

skill.description: The exact name of the skill to invoke, spelled as it appears in the current skill listing (e.g. "commit", "pdf").

args.description: Optional argument string for the skill, written like a command line (e.g. `-m "fix bug"`, `123`, a file path). It is split on whitespace (quotes group a token) and expanded into the skill's placeholders ($NAME, $1, $ARGUMENTS); if the skill body has no placeholders, the whole string is still appended as a trailing `ARGUMENTS:` line. Omit it only when there is nothing to pass.

tools.name: TaskList
tools.description:
List background tasks and their current status.

Use this tool to discover which background tasks exist and where each one
stands. It is the entry point for inspecting background work: it returns a
task ID, status, and description for every task it reports, plus the command,
PID, and (once finished) exit code for shell tasks, and a stop reason for any
task that ended early.

Guidelines:

- After a context compaction, or whenever you are unsure which background
  tasks are running or what their task IDs are, call this tool to
  re-enumerate them instead of guessing a task ID.
- Prefer the default `active_only=true`, which lists only non-terminal tasks.
  Pass `active_only=false` only when you specifically need to see tasks that
  have already finished. With `active_only=false` the result may also include
  `lost` tasks — tasks left over from a previous process that can no longer be
  inspected or controlled; treat them as already terminated.
- `limit` caps how many tasks are returned. It accepts a value between 1 and
  100 and defaults to 20 when omitted.
- This tool only lists tasks; it does not return their output. Use it first
  to locate the task ID you need, then call `TaskOutput` with that ID to read
  the task's output and details.
- This tool is read-only and does not change any state, so it is always safe
  to call, including in plan mode.

active_only.description: Whether to list only non-terminal background tasks.

limit.description: Maximum number of tasks to return.

tools.name: TaskOutput
tools.description:
Retrieve a snapshot of a running or completed background task.

Use this after `Bash(run_in_background=true)` or `Agent(run_in_background=true)` to check progress, or to read the output of a task that has already completed.

Guidelines:
- Prefer relying on automatic completion notifications. Use this tool only when you need task output before the automatic notification arrives.
- By default this tool is non-blocking and returns a current status/output snapshot — that is the normal way to use it.
- Do not use TaskOutput to wait for a result you need before continuing — if your next step depends on the task's result, run that task in the foreground instead. TaskOutput is for a deliberate progress check you will act on without blocking, not a way to sit and wait for a background task you just launched.
- Use block=true only when the user explicitly asked you to wait for the task. Never block on a task you launched in the current turn — if you need its result right away, it should have been a foreground call.
- If a block=true call returns `retrieval_status: timeout` (the task is still running), do not block on the same task again. Continue with other work or hand back to the user — the completion notification arrives on its own.
- This tool returns structured task metadata, a fixed-size output preview, and an output_path for the full log.
- For a terminal task, the metadata also explains why it ended. A shell command that runs to completion reports `status: completed` on a zero exit, or `status: failed` with its non-zero `exit_code` — judge that failure from the `exit_code`, because a plain command failure carries no `stop_reason` and no `terminal_reason`. `terminal_reason` is a categorical label emitted only when the end is not an ordinary exit: `timed_out` when the deadline aborted it, `stopped` when it was explicitly stopped, or `failed` when it errored without producing an exit code; the `stopped` and `failed` cases also carry a human-readable `stop_reason`. A task that finished on its own with a clean exit carries neither `stop_reason` nor `terminal_reason`.
- The full, never-truncated log is always available at output_path; use the `Read` tool with that path to page through it, whether or not the preview was truncated.
- This tool works with the generic background task system and should remain the primary read path for future task types, not just bash.

task_id.description: The background task ID to inspect.

block.description: Whether to wait for the task to finish before returning. Discouraged — background tasks notify automatically on completion; use only when the user explicitly asked you to wait.

timeout.description: Maximum number of seconds to wait when block=true.

tools.name: TaskStop
tools.description:
Stop a running background task.

Only use this when a task must genuinely be cancelled — for a task that is
finishing normally, wait for its completion notification or inspect it with
`TaskOutput` instead of stopping it.

Guidelines:
- This is a general-purpose stop capability for any background task. It is not
  a bash-specific kill.
- Stopping a task is destructive: it may leave partial side effects behind.
  Use it with care.
- If the task has already finished, this tool simply returns its current
  status.

task_id.description: The background task ID to stop.

reason.description: Short reason recorded when the task is stopped.

tools.name: TodoList
tools.description:
Use this tool to maintain a structured TODO list as you work through a multi-step task. Use it proactively and often when progress tracking helps the current work. This is especially useful in long-running investigations and implementation tasks with several tool calls; in plan mode, write the plan to the plan file rather than tracking it here.

**When to use:**
- Multi-step tasks that span several tool calls
- Tracking investigation progress across a large codebase search
- Planning a sequence of edits before making them
- After receiving new multi-step instructions, capture the requirements as todos
- Before starting a tracked task, mark exactly one item as `in_progress`
- Immediately after finishing a tracked task, mark it `done`; do not batch completions at the end

**When NOT to use:**

# ydata-profiling

**One line of code. A complete picture of your data.**

`ydata-profiling` generates rich, interactive profile reports from pandas
(and Spark) DataFrames. For each column it computes the inferred type,
descriptive statistics, the most frequent values, and a histogram, and for
the dataset as a whole it surfaces missing values, duplicate rows, and
correlations between variables.

```python
import pandas as pd
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

df = pd.read_csv("my_data.csv")
profile = ProfileReport(df, title="My data report")
profile.to_file("report.html")
```

The resulting HTML report is self-contained and can be shared with anyone,
embedded in notebooks, or exported as JSON for programmatic consumption.

## Why profiling?

Exploratory data analysis is the first step of every data science workflow,
and also the most repetitive. Writing the same `df.describe()`, null counts,
and distribution plots for every new dataset is slow and error-prone.
ydata-profiling automates this boilerplate so you can spend your time
interpreting the data instead of summarizing it, and it catches data quality
issues — high cardinality, skewness, constant columns, unexpected
correlations — that ad-hoc inspection routinely misses.

# Overview

ydata-profiling is the successor of `pandas-profiling`, the widely used
library for exploratory data analysis of pandas DataFrames. It extends the
original project with support for time series datasets, dataset comparison,
Spark DataFrames, and an improved report design, while keeping the familiar
one-line API.

## Key capabilities

- **Type inference**: columns are automatically detected as numeric,
  categorical, boolean, date, text, URL, file path, or image, and each type
  gets statistics appropriate to it.
- **Data quality alerts**: the report flags constant and duplicated columns,
  high cardinality, heavy skewness, missing values, and more.
- **Correlations**: Spearman, Pearson, Kendall, Cramér's V, and Phik (φk)
  correlation matrices, with automatic selection available.
- **Dataset comparison**: side-by-side reports for two or more datasets,
  useful for train/test drift analysis.
- **Scalability**: sampling, minimal mode, and Spark support for datasets
  that do not fit comfortably in memory.
- **Flexible output**: interactive HTML, embeddable widgets for Jupyter, and
  JSON for machine-readable pipelines.

## Compatibility

ydata-profiling supports Python 3.9 and later, and pandas versions from 1.1
up to (but not including) 3.0. For backwards compatibility, the package can
also be imported as `pandas_profiling`:

```python
import ydata_profiling  # preferred
import pandas_profiling  # legacy alias, still works
```

# Concepts

Understanding a few core concepts makes it much easier to configure
ydata-profiling effectively.

## Type inference with visions

ydata-profiling does not rely on pandas dtypes alone. It uses the
[visions](https://github.com/dylan-profiler/visions) type system to infer the
*semantic* type of each column — a string column may be detected as
categorical, text, a URL, or a file path; an integer column may really be a
boolean or a date. The inferred type determines which statistics are
computed: text columns get character and word distributions, URLs get domain
counts, images get dimension and EXIF summaries.

## The report structure

A report is organised into sections:

- **Overview**: dataset-level statistics (number of variables, rows, missing
  cells, duplicates, memory usage) and data quality alerts.
- **Variables**: one expandable block per column with descriptive statistics,
  a histogram or frequency plot, and type-specific details.
- **Interactions**: scatter plots of pairs of variables (disabled by default
  for wide datasets).
- **Correlations**: heatmaps for the configured correlation metrics.
- **Missing values**: counts, matrix, and (for smaller datasets) dendrogram
  views of missingness.
- **Sample**: the first and last rows of the dataset, and duplicate rows
  when present.

## Configuration model

All behaviour is controlled by a hierarchical settings object
(`ydata_profiling.config.Settings`), loaded from YAML. Settings can be
overridden per report — either with keyword arguments
(`ProfileReport(df, minimal=True)`), by mutating
`profile.config`, or by loading a custom YAML file. See
[changing settings](../advanced_settings/changing_settings.md) for details.

## Descriptions as data

Internally, rendering a report is a two-step process: first the dataset is
*described* into a plain dictionary of statistics, then that description is
*rendered* to HTML, widgets, or JSON. You can hook into the first step with
`profile.get_description()` to build your own tooling on top of the computed
statistics.

# Profiling big data

Datasets with millions of rows or hundreds of columns can make a full
profile slow to compute and heavy to render. ydata-profiling offers several
strategies, roughly in order of preference.

## Minimal mode

`minimal=True` disables the most expensive computations — correlations,
interactions, and several detailed per-variable statistics — while keeping
the essentials: types, missing values, duplicates, and descriptive
statistics.

```python
profile = ProfileReport(large_df, minimal=True, title="Large dataset")
```

This is the first thing to try: it is often several times faster than the
default configuration and is usually enough for a first look at a big table.

## Sampling

Instead of computing over the full dataset, profile a representative sample:

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df, sample={"name": "10% sample", "frac": 0.1})
```

or a fixed number of rows:

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df, sample={"name": "10k rows", "n": 10000})
```

The report notes the sample size so readers know the statistics are
estimates. Sampling preserves the row order of the underlying draw, so for
time-ordered data prefer shuffling first or use `tsmode`.

## Per-computation tuning

For finer control, disable individual expensive sections:

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df)
profile.config.interactions.continuous = False
profile.config.correlations = {}          # skip all correlation matrices
profile.config.missing_diagrams = {}      # skip missing-value diagrams
```

Correlations are quadratic in the number of numeric columns, so dropping
them matters most on wide tables. See
[available settings](../advanced_settings/available_settings.md) for the
full list of knobs.

## Spark

When the data does not fit on one machine at all, profile a Spark DataFrame
directly — ydata-profiling computes the statistics in the Spark cluster.
See the [PySpark integration](../integrations/pyspark.md).

# Comparing datasets

`ydata_profiling.compare` places two or more reports side by side, making it
easy to spot distribution drift between a training and a production
snapshot, before/after a data cleaning step, or any pair of related tables.

## Basic usage

```python
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport, compare

train_report = ProfileReport(train_df, title="Train")
prod_report = ProfileReport(prod_df, title="Production")

comparison = compare([train_report, prod_report])
comparison.to_file("comparison.html")
```

The resulting report shows each statistic and histogram for both datasets
overlaid, so differences in distributions, missingness, and cardinality are
visible at a glance.

## Comparing more than two datasets

Pass any number of reports; labelling each one keeps the output readable:

```python
reports = [
    ProfileReport(df_jan, title="January"),
    ProfileReport(df_feb, title="February"),
    ProfileReport(df_mar, title="March"),
]
compare(reports).to_file("quarterly_drift.html")
```

## Tips

- Use the same configuration for all reports being compared — different
  correlation settings or bin counts make side-by-side plots misleading.
  The simplest approach is to build all reports from one shared config.
- Comparison works on the *description* level, so you can also compare JSON
  exports produced at different times or on different machines.
- For large datasets, profile samples of each dataset with the same random
  seed strategy so the comparison is fair.

See `examples/features/eda_dataset_compare.py` for a runnable demo.

# Metadata and dataset descriptions

A profile is far more useful when it records *what* the data is and *where
it came from*. ydata-profiling lets you attach this metadata to the report
instead of keeping it in a separate document nobody reads.

## Dataset metadata

```python
profile = ProfileReport(
    df,
    title="Customer churn extract",
    dataset={
        "description": "Monthly snapshot of active customers joined with churn labels.",
        "creator": "Analytics Engineering",
        "author": "J. Doe",
        "copyright_holder": "Example Corp",
        "copyright_year": "2026",
        "url": "https://data.example.com/catalog/churn",
    },
)
```

All fields are optional; provided ones are rendered in the overview section
and included in JSON exports, so downstream tooling can pick them up.

## Column descriptions

Human-readable explanations per column live under
`variables.descriptions`:

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df, title="Annotated report")
profile.config.variables.descriptions = {
    "tenure_months": "Number of months the customer has been active.",
    "churn": "1 if the customer cancelled within the period.",
}
```

Descriptions appear next to the variable statistics — especially valuable
for cryptic column names inherited from source systems.

## Why bother?

Profiling reports tend to outlive the analysis that produced them: they get
attached to tickets, linked from data catalogues, and rediscovered months
later. Embedding provenance and semantics in the report itself means the
context travels with the statistics, and the JSON export doubles as a
machine-readable data dictionary.

# Handling sensitive data

Reports often get shared more widely than the raw data. A single HTML file
containing names, identifiers, or rare value combinations can leak more
than intended, so ydata-profiling provides a *sensitive mode*.

## Sensitive mode

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df, title="HR extract (anonymized)", sensitive=True)
```

With `sensitive=True`:

- the **Samples** section (head, tail, and duplicate rows) is omitted, so
  no raw records appear in the report;
- category-level detail for categorical and text columns is reduced.

Statistics such as counts, means, and histograms are still computed — the
report remains useful for understanding distributions without exposing
individual records.

## What sensitive mode is *not*

Sensitive mode reduces disclosure risk; it is not anonymization. Aggregate
statistics can still reveal information about small groups (e.g. a category
with a single member). Before sharing a report on genuinely confidential
data:

1. Drop or hash direct identifiers (emails, national IDs) from the DataFrame
   *before* profiling.
2. Review high-cardinality columns — unique values are listed in frequency
   tables.
3. Consider reporting on a sample so exact counts are not recoverable.

## Combining with other settings

Sensitive mode composes with the rest of the configuration. A common
pattern is a shareable "external" report and a full internal one:

```python
external = ProfileReport(df, title="External", sensitive=True, minimal=True)
internal = ProfileReport(df, title="Internal")
```

See `examples/features/mask_sensitive.py` for a runnable example.

# Time series datasets

Standard profiling assumes rows are exchangeable. For time series that
assumption is wrong — order matters — so ydata-profiling has a dedicated
time series mode.

## Enabling time series mode

```python
profile = ProfileReport(
    df,
    tsmode=True,
    sortby="timestamp",
    title="Air quality over time",
)
```

Two things change in `tsmode`:

- **Line plots replace histograms** for the overview of numeric variables,
  showing each series against row order (or the sorted timestamp) so trends,
  seasonality, and regime shifts are visible.
- **Autocorrelation plots** (ACF/PACF) are added per numeric variable, which
  help spot lag structure before modelling.

`sortby` accepts a column name or a list of columns; sort before profiling
if the DataFrame index order is not chronological.

## Choosing variables

Not every column benefits from the time series treatment. Identifier-like
columns are better left alone:

```python
profile.config.vars.num.low_categorical_threshold = 5
profile.config.timeseries.active = True
```

The `timeseries` settings group controls which variables get the line-plot
and autocorrelation treatment.

## Practical notes

- Keep the series contiguous where possible; large gaps make the line plots
  misleading. Resampling to a regular frequency first often produces a
  clearer report.
- For very long series, combine `tsmode` with a
  [sample](big_data.md#sampling) taken as a contiguous window rather than a
  random fraction, so the ordering information is preserved.
- A runnable example is `examples/usaairquality/usaairquality.py`.

# Available settings

All report behaviour is driven by a hierarchical settings tree, defined in
`ydata_profiling.config.Settings` (a pydantic model, so unknown keys and
wrong types fail loudly). This page maps out the main branches; the
defaults live in
`src/ydata_profiling/config_default.yaml` in the repository.

## Top-level options

| Setting | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `title` | `"Pandas Profiling Report"` | Report title shown in the header |
| `minimal` | `False` | Cheapest useful profile: no correlations, interactions, or detailed plots |
| `sensitive` | `False` | Omit samples and category detail (see [sensitive data](../features/sensitive_data.md)) |
| `tsmode` | `False` | Time series mode: line plots and autocorrelation |
| `explorative` | `False` | Opposite of minimal: enables everything, including interactions |
| `sample` | `None` | Dict like `{"name": ..., "n": ...}` or `{"frac": ...}` to profile a sample |
| `sortby` | `None` | Column(s) to sort by before profiling |
| `dark_mode` / `orange_mode` | `False` | Built-in colour schemes |

## Branch highlights

- **`vars.num` / `vars.cat` / `vars.text`** — bin counts, quantile lists,
  low-categorical thresholds, and per-type toggles.
- **`correlations`** — one sub-setting per metric: `pearson`, `spearman`,
  `kendall`, `cramers`, `phi_k`, plus `auto` which picks per column type.
  Each has `calculate` and a `threshold`/`warn` level used for alerts.
- **`interactions`** — `continuous` toggles pairwise scatter plots (off by
  default; quadratic cost).
- **`missing_diagrams`** — `matrix`, `bar`, `heatmap`, `dendrogram` toggles.
- **`plot`** — DPI, image format (`png`/`svg`), histogram binning, and
  correlation plot arguments.
- **`html.style`** — `theme`, `primary_color`, `logo`, `full_width`; see
  [custom reports](../features/custom_reports.md).
- **`duplicates` / `samples`** — how many duplicate rows and head/tail rows
  to include.
- **`dataset` / `variables.descriptions`** — metadata covered in
  [metadata](../features/metadata.md).
- **`n_obs_unique` / `n_freq_table_max`** — caps that keep rendering
  tractable on high-cardinality data.
- **`progress_bar`, `pool_size`** — UI and parallelism controls.

## Inspecting the effective configuration

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df)
print(profile.config.json(indent=2))  # the full resolved settings tree
```

Because settings are a pydantic model, `config.json()` is a reliable way to
see exactly what a report used — handy when filing bug reports.

# Changing settings

There are four ways to change the configuration, from most common to most
powerful. They can be combined; later overrides win.

## 1. Constructor shorthands

The most common options are keyword arguments on `ProfileReport`:

```python
profile = ProfileReport(
    df,
    title="Sales data",
    minimal=True,
    explorative=False,
    sensitive=False,
    dark_mode=False,
    sample={"name": "10k sample", "n": 10000},
)
```

## 2. Mutating `profile.config`

Anything in the settings tree can be changed through attribute assignment.
Because the tree is validated by pydantic, typos raise immediately:

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df, title="Customised")
profile.config.vars.num.n_quantiles = 100
profile.config.plot.histogram.bins = 50
profile.config.correlations["spearman"].calculate = False
profile.config.html.style.primary_color = "#2a9d8f"
```

## 3. YAML configuration files

For reproducible, shareable setups, keep settings in a YAML file:

```yaml
# config_minimal.yaml
title: "Warehouse snapshot"
minimal: true
plot:
  dpi: 150
  image_format: svg
correlations:
  kendall:
    calculate: false
```

```python
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

profile = ProfileReport(df, config_file="config_minimal.yaml")
```

The file is merged over the defaults, so you only specify what changes.

## 4. Loading and dumping `Settings` directly

```python
from ydata_profiling.config import Settings

settings = Settings()
settings.minimal = True
profile = ProfileReport(df, config=settings)

# Round-trip through JSON for storage:
restored = Settings.parse_raw(settings.json())
```

## Recommendations

- Put shared organisation-wide defaults in a committed YAML file and pass it
  via `config_file`; keep one-off tweaks as constructor arguments.
- When reporting a bug, attach `profile.config.json()` output so
  maintainers can reproduce the exact configuration.

# Caching

Profiling recomputes statistics every time a report is built. During an
iterative session — tweaking settings, re-rendering, comparing outputs —
this gets slow. ydata-profiling caches intermediate results on disk so
repeated runs only redo what changed.

## How it works

Expensive computations (per-variable descriptions, correlation matrices)
are memoized through [joblib](https://joblib.readthedocs.io/)'s `Memory`.
The cache key covers the input data and the relevant settings, so changing
a setting invalidates only the parts that depend on it.

## Choosing the cache location

By default a temporary directory is used. Point it somewhere persistent to
share the cache across processes and reboots:

```python
from joblib import Memory
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

profile = ProfileReport(df, title="Cached run")
profile.config.vars.low_categorical_threshold = 0  # example tweak
```

Set the cache directory via the `YDATA_PROFILING_CACHE_DIR`-style
environment/joblib configuration, or construct a `Memory` instance and use
it when building your own pipelines around `get_description()`.

## When caching helps — and when it does not

- **Helps**: repeated reports over the same DataFrame while iterating on
  settings; CI jobs that regenerate the same reports.
- **Does not help**: one-off reports; data that changes every run (the
  cache key includes the data, so new data means a cold cache).

## Housekeeping

The cache is not size-managed automatically. If you use a persistent
directory, clear it periodically:

```python
memory = Memory(".cache/ydata_profiling", verbose=0)
memory.clear()
```

Keep the cache directory out of version control — add it to `.gitignore`.

# Analytics and telemetry

ydata-profiling can emit anonymous usage events that help the maintainers
understand which features are used and where the library is slow or
fragile. This page explains what is collected and how to opt out.

## What is collected

Events are coarse-grained and contain **no data**: things like "a report was
generated with N rows and M columns", which optional features were enabled
(`tsmode`, `sensitive`, `minimal`), how long rendering took, and the
library/Python versions. Column names, values, and report contents are
never included.

## Opting out

Telemetry is off unless explicitly enabled. If your environment has it on
(for example via an organisation-wide configuration), disable it by setting
the environment variable before importing:

```bash
export YDATA_PROFILING_NO_ANALYTICS=true
```

or programmatically:

```python
import os
os.environ["YDATA_PROFILING_NO_ANALYTICS"] = "true"

from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport  # import after setting the flag
```

When analytics are disabled, no network calls are made during profiling.

## Checking your environment

In locked-down environments (no outbound network), analytics silently
no-op; report generation does not depend on them. If you see unexpected
network traffic, verify the flag above is set in the environment of the
process actually running Python — notebook kernels and schedulers often
have their own environment.

# Caching

This page covers the two kinds of caching relevant to ydata-profiling:
the built-in dataset download cache, and caching *you* add around report
generation for repeated runs.

## Built-in dataset cache

The helper functions used by the example scripts and tutorials
(`ydata_profiling.utils.cache.cache_file` and `cache_zipped_file`) download
a dataset over HTTP once and store it in a local data directory. On
subsequent calls the cached file is reused instead of downloading again:

```python
from ydata_profiling.utils.cache import cache_file

path = cache_file("titanic.csv", "https://example.org/titanic.csv")
```

The cache location is resolved by `ydata_profiling.utils.paths.get_data_path()`
— a `data/` directory in the current working context. Delete that directory
to force re-downloads, and keep it out of version control.

Note that the profiling computation itself (descriptive statistics,
correlations, plots) is **not** memoized by the library: every
`ProfileReport(...)` call recomputes from the DataFrame it is given.

## Caching report outputs yourself

When you regenerate the same report repeatedly — nightly jobs, CI, notebook
re-runs — cache at the *artifact* level instead:

- **HTML/JSON exports**: store `profile.to_file(...)` output keyed by a hash
  of the input data and the configuration (`profile.config.json()` is a
  stable serialization of the settings). If the key matches, skip the
  computation entirely.
- **Descriptions**: `profile.get_description()` returns a plain dictionary
  that is cheap to pickle and reload:

```python
import hashlib
import pickle

import pandas as pd
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

def cached_description(df: pd.DataFrame, cache_dir=".cache/profiling"):
    key = hashlib.sha256(pd.util.hash_pandas_object(df).values).hexdigest()
    path = f"{cache_dir}/{key}.pkl"
    try:
        with open(path, "rb") as f:
            return pickle.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        import os
        os.makedirs(cache_dir, exist_ok=True)
        desc = ProfileReport(df, minimal=True).get_description()
        with open(path, "wb") as f:
            pickle.dump(desc, f)
        return desc
```

## Practical notes

- Include the library version in the cache key — statistics and schema can
  change between releases, making stale caches misleading.
- For [dataset comparison](../features/comparing_datasets.md), caching the
  per-dataset descriptions lets you compare a new snapshot against many
  historical ones without recomputing them.

# Analytics and usage data

This page summarizes what the library does (and does not do) with respect
to analytics and outbound network calls, and how to keep report generation
fully offline.

## What ydata-profiling sends

The core profiling pipeline — describing a DataFrame and rendering a
report — makes **no network calls**. Statistics are computed locally from
the DataFrame you pass in, and the HTML report inlines all of its assets
(CSS, JavaScript, images as base64), so viewing a report does not phone
home either.

Network access only happens when your own code triggers it, typically:

- downloading example datasets with
  `ydata_profiling.utils.cache.cache_file` / `cache_zipped_file`;
- loading data yourself with `pandas.read_csv("https://...")`-style URLs.

## Keeping it fully offline

For air-gapped or compliance-sensitive environments:

1. Provide data locally (files, databases) rather than via URLs.
2. Ship fonts and viewer assets with the report — the default self-contained
   HTML already does this, so no extra step is needed.
3. If you distribute reports externally, review them before sharing:
   frequency tables and sample rows can contain identifying values. See
   [sensitive data](../features/sensitive_data.md) for the built-in
   `sensitive=True` mode.

## Verifying locally

You can confirm the offline behaviour empirically: generate a report inside
a network namespace without connectivity, or simply run with networking
disabled for the process — report generation succeeds either way, because
nothing in the render path requires it.

## Questions

If you observe unexpected network activity during profiling, please open an
issue with the ydata-profiling version, your configuration
(`profile.config.json()`), and a description of the traffic so the
maintainers can investigate.

# PySpark integration

For datasets that live in a Spark cluster, ydata-profiling can profile a
Spark DataFrame directly — statistics are computed with Spark operations,
so the data never needs to fit in the driver's memory.

## Installation

```bash
pip install "ydata-profiling[spark]"
```

This installs `pyspark` and `pyarrow`. A working Java runtime is required
for local Spark sessions.

## Usage

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[*]").getOrCreate()
sdf = spark.read.parquet("s3://bucket/events/")

profile = ProfileReport(sdf, title="Events (Spark)")
profile.to_file("events_report.html")
```

`ProfileReport` detects the Spark DataFrame type and dispatches to the
Spark backend automatically — the API is identical to the pandas case, and
so is the resulting report.

## Notes and limitations

- Spark profiling computes most of the same statistics as the pandas
  backend, but a few pandas-specific details (certain interactions and
  diagram types) may differ or be unavailable. Check the alerts section of
  the generated report for anything that was skipped.
- Sampling still helps: `sample={"frac": 0.1}` translates into a Spark
  `sample`, reducing shuffle and compute time on very large tables.
- Cache (`sdf.cache()`) a DataFrame before profiling if it is the result of
  a long lineage — profiling triggers multiple passes over the data.
- A runnable example is `examples/features/spark_example.py`.

# Great Expectations integration

ydata-profiling answers "what does my data look like?"; Great Expectations
answers "does my data satisfy the rules I care about?". The two compose
naturally: profile first to understand the data, then turn what you learn
into expectations.

## Generating an expectation suite from a profile

The integration builds a Great Expectations suite from the statistics a
report already computed:

```python
import great_expectations as gx
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

profile = ProfileReport(df, title="Orders", minimal=True, explorative=False)

suite = profile.to_expectation_suite(
    suite_name="orders_suite",
    data_context_type="ephemeral",
    run_validation=True,
    build_suite=True,
)
```

The generated suite encodes expectations derived from the observed data:
column existence and types, null fractions, value ranges for numeric
columns, and sets of observed categories for low-cardinality columns.

## Prerequisites

The integration requires `great_expectations` (install it separately; it is
not a core dependency) and pandas. Save the suite with a real
`DataContext` when you want it to persist:

```python
context = gx.get_context()
context.add_or_update_expectation_suite(expectation_suite=suite)
```

## Typical workflow

1. **Profile** a trusted snapshot (e.g. last month's data) to learn ranges,
   categories, and nullability.
2. **Generate** the expectation suite from that profile.
3. **Hand-tune** the suite — generated expectations describe what *was*,
   not necessarily what *should be*; tighten bounds based on domain
   knowledge.
4. **Validate** new batches against the suite in your pipeline, and
   re-profile periodically to detect drift the expectations do not cover.

# IDE integrations

ydata-profiling works in any Python environment, but a few integrations
make the loop tighter in the tools people actually use.

## Jupyter and JupyterLab

The first-class environment. Render reports inline:

```python
profile.to_notebook_iframe()   # iframe-embedded HTML
profile.to_widgets()           # interactive ipywidgets version
```

`to_widgets()` requires the `notebook` extra
(`pip install "ydata-profiling[notebook]"`) and ipywidgets enabled in the
frontend. The iframe variant works everywhere HTML output is supported,
including JupyterLab, VS Code notebooks, and Google Colab.

## VS Code

In VS Code notebooks, `to_notebook_iframe()` renders in the cell output.
For standalone scripts, write the report to a file and open it with the
built-in preview or Live Preview extension:

```python
profile.to_file("report.html")
```

The repository ships a `.devcontainer` with the Python extension, black,
and pytest preconfigured — open the folder in a container to get a
ready-made development environment.

## PyCharm

PyCharm's Scientific mode displays DataFrames and supports notebook cells,
where the iframe output works as in Jupyter. For script runs, generate the
HTML file and use *Open in Browser*. Set the matplotlib backend to `Agg`
in headless run configurations to avoid GUI backend issues.

## Other editors

Any editor works: the report is a plain HTML file. A small helper keeps the
flow fast:

```python
import webbrowser
profile.to_file("report.html")
webbrowser.open("report.html")
```

# Pipeline integrations

Profiling fits naturally into data pipelines as a data-quality gate or an
observability artifact. The library is orchestrator-agnostic — it is just a
Python call — but a few patterns work well across Airflow, Dagster,
Prefect, Luigi, and plain cron.

## Pattern: profile as a task artifact

Generate a report for every materialized table and store the HTML as a task
artifact (S3, GCS, or the orchestrator's artifact store):

```python
def profile_task(df, output_uri, run_id):
    profile = ProfileReport(
        df,
        title=f"orders @ {run_id}",
        minimal=True,  # keep runtime predictable in pipelines
    )
    profile.to_file(output_uri)
```

Minimal mode keeps runtime and memory bounded, which matters when the task
shares a worker with other jobs.

## Pattern: JSON export for machine checks

When the pipeline should *react* to the data, export JSON and assert on
statistics instead of eyeballing HTML:

```python
desc = ProfileReport(df, minimal=True).get_description()
table = desc["table"]

assert table["n_cells_missing"] == 0, "unexpected missing values"
assert table["n_duplicates"] / table["n"] < 0.01, "duplicate spike"
```

For declarative checks on top of this, see the
[Great Expectations integration](great_expectations.md).

## Pattern: drift monitoring with compare

Keep the previous period's report description and
[compare](../features/comparing_datasets.md) the new batch against it;
large divergences in distributions are an early warning for upstream
schema or feed changes.

## Operational tips

- Set `progress_bar=False` so logs stay clean.
- Profile a deterministic [sample](../features/big_data.md#sampling) for
  very large tables; document the sample in the report title.
- Treat the library version as part of the pipeline contract: pin it, since
  statistics and report schema can evolve between releases.

# Changelog

All notable changes to ydata-profiling are documented here. The format
follows [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.0.0/) and the
project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/). Releases are
produced by semantic-release from
[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/).

The authoritative, per-release list of changes is on the
[GitHub releases page](https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling/releases).

## [4.16.1]

### Fixed

- Compatibility fixes for recent numpy and pandas releases.
- Minor report rendering corrections.

## [4.16.0]

### Added

- Continued improvements to the Spark backend and time series mode.

## Migrating from pandas-profiling

If you are coming from `pandas-profiling` 3.x, the breaking changes are
concentrated in the 4.0 release:

- Package renamed to `ydata-profiling` (`import ydata_profiling`; the
  legacy `import pandas_profiling` alias is still provided).
- Configuration system rewritten on top of pydantic — most setting keys are
  unchanged, but validation is stricter.
- `df.profile_report()` remains available as a pandas accessor.

See the [history page](history.md) for the full story of the rename.

# History

## Origins

The project started in 2016 as **pandas-profiling**, created by Jos Polfliet
and subsequently maintained by Simon Brugman. The idea was simple: the
`df.describe()` one-liner was useful but far too shallow, and every data
scientist was rewriting the same exploratory boilerplate. pandas-profiling
turned that boilerplate into a single call producing a rich HTML report.

Over the following years the project grew to millions of downloads and
became a default step in exploratory data analysis, adding correlation
metrics (including Phik), missing-value diagrams, dataset comparison, and
configurable report styling.

## The move to YData

In 2022 the project joined [YData](https://ydata.ai) and was renamed
**ydata-profiling**, starting with version 4.0. The rename came with a
modernized codebase:

- configuration rebuilt on pydantic models with strict validation;
- a pluggable backend architecture, enabling support beyond pandas —
  notably Apache Spark DataFrames;
- time series mode (`tsmode`) with line plots and autocorrelation;
- continued compatibility via the `pandas_profiling` import alias and CLI.

## Today

ydata-profiling remains MIT-licensed open source, developed in the open at
[github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling](https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling).
It is maintained by YData together with community contributors — see the
[contribution guidelines](../support-contribution/contribution_guidelines.md)
if you would like to get involved, and [resources](resources.md) for talks,
articles, and related projects.

# Resources

Pointers to material that helps you get more out of ydata-profiling.

## Code and community

- **Source code and issue tracker**:
  [github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling](https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling)
- **PyPI package**: [pypi.org/project/ydata-profiling](https://pypi.org/project/ydata-profiling/)
- **Discord community**: [discord.ydata.ai](https://discord.ydata.ai) —
  the fastest way to get usage questions answered.

## Examples

The [examples directory](https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling/tree/develop/examples)
in the repository contains runnable scripts for every major feature:
standard datasets (Titanic, census, meteorites), dataset comparison,
sensitive-data masking, theming, Spark, image and URL types, and time
series profiling. The [examples page](../getting-started/examples.md) lists
them with a one-line description each.

## Related projects in the ecosystem

- **YData Fabric / synthetic data**: generate privacy-preserving synthetic
  data informed by profiling statistics.
- **visions**: the semantic type system ydata-profiling uses for type
  inference ([github.com/dylan-profiler/visions](https://github.com/dylan-profiler/visions)).
- **phik**: the φk correlation library used for mixed-type correlation
  matrices.
- **Great Expectations**: data validation that pairs well with profiling —
  see the [integration guide](../integrations/great_expectations.md).

## Citing

If ydata-profiling contributes to academic work, please cite the repository
and the version used. Including `ydata_profiling.__version__` in your
methods section makes analyses reproducible.
